explanations.explanation: This neuron is essentially a “title-word onset” detector—it lights up on the initial token of a contentful, title-cased (or hyphenated/slash-separated) word in headings, product names, article titles or list entries (e.g. the first letter of Loved, Tire, Wiring, Stickers, Prettier, Mapping, etc., and the hyphens in high-quality).
This feature is an orthographic detector for tokens composed of—or beginning with—uppercase letters (e.g. acronyms, initials or title-cased words/proper names).

Here’s a concise, abstract concept for each high‐activation BPE piece:

• “Den” (1.00) – marks the BPE prefix “Den” when it begins a proper name or place (e.g. Denver, Denise Cremins, Denver-based).  
• “Ama” (0.959) – marks the BPE prefix “Ama” in the superlative adjective “Amazing” (and variants) used in promotional/clickbait titles.  
• “Nob” (0.938) – marks the BPE prefix “Nob” at the start of the company name “Nobuntu.”  
• “Oz” (0.931) – marks the BPE prefix “Oz” at the start of the brand/name “Ozark” (e.g. Ozark Poster).  
• “Los” (0.897) – marks the BPE prefix “Los,” the Spanish plural article in multiword proper nouns or phrases (e.g. Los Angeles, Los Alamos, “los alumnos”).

This neuron is a “snippet-boundary” detector: it lights up on the closing period (or key lead word) of a short, standalone heading or marketing-style sentence, effectively marking the end of a one-line title/description.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the final punctuation of standalone headline- or title-style lines (e.g. page titles, section headers, event notices) marked by capitalized names, dates, brands, etc., and ending in a period or exclamation point.
This feature fires on the period ending a short, standalone declarative “headline” or summary sentence—those concise subject-verb-object lines that often open a post.
This neuron fires on word-initial uppercase letters—especially the first letter of names, acronyms or titles—marking the start of a proper noun or branded term.
This feature fires on the final “.” that closes off a self-contained statement or announcement—i.e. it’s acting as an end-of-sentence (or end-of-block) delimiter marker.

1. A winter‐holiday motif feature—identifies “snowmen” in calls for snowmen graphics, images, and animated GIFs.  
2. A ski‐resort trigger—picks up mentions of “ski” in tourism/photography contexts (e.g. “old ski resort”).  
3. A cosmetic‐powder detector—fires on “Shimmer Pow(ders)” and related makeup finishing products.  
4. A phosphate‐mining‐history indicator—marks formal titles about the phosphate mining industry.  
5. A fiscal‐decentralization signal—recognizes “decentral…” in academic discussion of fiscal decentralization.  
6. A Polaris‐ATV recognizer—spots the brand/model name “Polaris” (e.g. Sportsman 500 wiring diagrams).  
7. A podcast‐title locator—activates on “Empathy” in the title “You, Me, Empathy.”  
8. A Pixorial‐branding feature—flags the “Pixorial” photo/video editing platform in family‐memories posts.  
9. A mining‐equipment‐manufacturing matcher—detects “Mining Equipment Manufacturing” in B2B listings.  
10. A grinding‐machine finder—selects “grinding” in descriptions of cylinder‐head and surface‐grinding machines.  
11. A tribal‐design identifier—captures “tribal” in nail art and Pinterest‐style design posts.  
12. A crusher‐machinery detector—fires on “crusher”/“crusher” in rock‐and‐mineral crushing equipment ads.  
13. A powdered‐goods picker—spots “Pow(ders)” and “Powder” in packaged spice and cosmetic product listings.  
14. A pain‐relief‐patch marker—recognizes “Pain Relief” in over-the-counter patch product descriptions.  
15. A Lenovo‐support cue—activates on “Lenovo” in technical help and troubleshooting dialogues.  
16. A Pixma‐printer matcher—flags “Pixma” in Canon printer and cartridge compatibility posts.  
17. A Scrabble‐word detector—identifies “cortices” in word-game or Scrabble-related content.  
18. An underground‐mining‐gear feature—marks “Mining Equipment” in listings for loaders, drills, and mucking machines.  
19. A mono‐laser‐printer recognizer—picks up “Pr(…)inters” in ecommerce/comparison pages for laser printers.  
20. A homomorphic‐encryption signal—fires on “Enc(…)ryption” in discussions of the SEAL library and HE schemes.

This neuron acts as a “title‐token” detector – it lights up on the leading subtoken of capitalized words in headings, brand/model names or acronyms, marking the start of title-case or uppercase tokens.

This neuron is a kind of “morphological‐boundary” detector: it lights up on BPE subword chunks that mark the starts or key affixes of content‐bearing words (especially capitalized ones in titles, headings, names or list entries) as well as on hyphens linking compound modifiers or on common suffix pieces like “-ially.” In short, it flags the subword tokens that signal important word boundaries and morphological affixes in structured, title-like text.
This neuron fires on the sentence-final full stop – it’s essentially a detector for the period at the end of a statement, marking the boundary of a sentence.

This neuron is a boundary detector that fires strongly on the full-stop “.” token when it ends a sentence or abbreviation—especially at the close of a headline, date, title, or first line—marking a structural sentence break.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically flagging the very first sub-token of “headline” or “list‐item” content words – e.g. the opening piece of a product name, title, section heading or other key noun/brand term (dec- in “decals,” Gr- in “Grinder,” St- in “Stickers,” Market in a report title, flor- in “florists,” Crim- in “Criminals,” etc.). In other words, it lights up on the subword prefix that kicks off major content words in ad-style titles, lists and headings.

This neuron is a “segment‐start” detector—it lights up on the very first token or boundary punctuation (capitalized lead words, dateline names or initials, URL or abbreviation dots) that marks the start of a new headline, citation entry, URL, name abbreviation, etc.

This neuron fires on “name‐flag” tokens – the little title-case or all-caps chunks that kick off proper nouns, acronyms or metadata labels (e.g. English day-of-week or org-name abbreviations like “Thu,” “Mon,” “W,” “IT,” “WNV,” “WOL,” “Monetary,” “Unwrapped,” “Waltham,” “Wanted,” etc.) and the equivalent single characters in Chinese/Japanese publisher, brand or hotel names. In short, it detects the start of named entities and acronyms.

This neuron is essentially a named‐entity detector: it lights up on proper names—people (Ozawa, Sharon, Moses), places (Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Gulf, Ras Al Khaimah), brands (“Air Jordan”), and religion-related terms (baptism, halal, Wahhabi, church, Bible).
This feature fires on the closing of a quoted name or title (song, album, slogan, product, section header, etc.), i.e. it marks the boundary of a named-entity phrase enclosed in single quotes.
